docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text: For the best performance, use these configurations and best practices:

docs.title: 1. Sampling Parameters
docs.text:
Use the following standardized sampling configuration across all use cases:

  • temperature=1.0
  • top_p=0.95
  • top_k=64

docs.title: 2. Thinking Mode Configuration
docs.text:
Compared to Gemma 3, the models use standard system, assistant, and user roles. To properly manage the thinking process, use the following control tokens:

  • Trigger Thinking: Thinking is enabled by including the <|think|> token at the start of the system prompt. To disable thinking, remove the token.
  • Standard Generation: When thinking is enabled, the model will output its internal reasoning followed by the final answer using this structure: <|channel>thought\n[Internal reasoning]<channel|>
  • Disabled Thinking Behavior: For all models except for the E2B and E4B variants, if thinking is disabled, the model will still generate the tags but with an empty thought block: <|channel>thought\n<channel|>[Final answer]

[!Note] Note that many libraries like Transformers and llama.cpp handle the complexities of the chat template for you.

docs.title: 3. Multi-Turn Conversations
docs.text: • No Thinking Content in History: In multi-turn conversations, the historical model output should only include the final response. Thoughts from previous model turns must not be added before the next user turn begins.

docs.title: 4. Modality order
docs.text:
For optimal performance with multimodal inputs, place:

  • Image content before the text in your prompt.
  • Audio content after the text in your prompt.

docs.title: 5. Variable Image Resolution
docs.text:
Aside from variable aspect ratios, Gemma 4 supports variable image resolution through a configurable visual token budget, which controls how many tokens are used to represent an image. A higher token budget preserves more visual detail at the cost of additional compute, while a lower budget enables faster inference for tasks that don't require fine-grained understanding.

  • The supported token budgets are: 70, 140, 280, 560, and 1120.
  • Use lower budgets for classification, captioning, or video understanding, where faster inference and processing many frames outweigh fine-grained detail.
  • Use higher budgets for tasks like OCR, document parsing, or reading small text.

docs.title: 6. Audio
docs.text:
Use the following prompt structures for audio processing:

  • Audio Speech Recognition (ASR)
Transcribe the following speech segment in {LANGUAGE} into {LANGUAGE} text.

Follow these specific instructions for formatting the answer:
* Only output the transcription, with no newlines.
* When transcribing numbers, write the digits, i.e. write 1.7 and not one point seven, and write 3 instead of three.
  • Automatic Speech Translation (AST)
Transcribe the following speech segment in {SOURCE_LANGUAGE}, then translate it into {TARGET_LANGUAGE}.
When formatting the answer, first output the transcription in {SOURCE_LANGUAGE}, then one newline, then output the string '{TARGET_LANGUAGE}: ', then the translation in {TARGET_LANGUAGE}.

docs.title: 7. Audio and Video Length
docs.text: All models support image inputs and can process videos as frames whereas the E2B, E4B, and 12B models also support audio inputs. Audio supports a maximum length of 30 seconds. Video supports a maximum of 60 seconds assuming the images are processed at one frame per second.

docs.title: Model Data
docs.text: Data used for model training and how the data was processed.

docs.title: Training Dataset
docs.text:
Our pre-training dataset is a large-scale, diverse collection of data encompassing a wide range of domains and modalities, which includes web documents, code, images, audio, with a cutoff date of January 2025. Here are the key components:

  • Web Documents: A diverse collection of web text ensures the model is exposed to a broad range of linguistic styles, topics, and vocabulary. The training dataset includes content in over 140 languages.
  • Code: Exposing the model to code helps it to learn the syntax and patterns of programming languages, which improves its ability to generate code and understand code-related questions.
  • Mathematics: Training on mathematical text helps the model learn logical reasoning, symbolic representation, and to address mathematical queries.
  • Images: A wide range of images enables the model to perform image analysis and visual data extraction tasks.

The combination of these diverse data sources is crucial for training a powerful multimodal model that can handle a wide variety of different tasks and data formats.

docs.title: Data Preprocessing
docs.text:
Here are the key data cleaning and filtering methods applied to the training data:

  • CSAM Filtering: Rigorous CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material) filtering was applied at multiple stages in the data preparation process to ensure the exclusion of harmful and illegal content.
  • Sensitive Data Filtering: As part of making Gemma pre-trained models safe and reliable, automated techniques were used to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets.
  • Additional methods: Filtering based on content quality and safety in line with our policies.

docs.title: Ethics and Safety
docs.text: As open models become central to enterprise infrastructure, provenance and security are paramount. Developed by Google DeepMind, Gemma 4 undergoes the same rigorous safety evaluations as our proprietary Gemini models.

docs.title: Evaluation Approach
docs.text:
Gemma 4 models were developed in partnership with internal safety and responsible AI teams. A range of automated as well as human evaluations were conducted to help improve model safety. These evaluations align with Googleâ€™s AI principles, as well as safety policies, which aim to prevent our generative AI models from generating harmful content, including:

  • Content related to child sexual abuse material and exploitation
  • Dangerous content (e.g., promoting suicide, or instructing in activities that could cause real-world harm)
  • Sexually explicit content
  • Hate speech (e.g., dehumanizing members of protected groups)
  • Harassment (e.g., encouraging violence against people)

docs.title: Evaluation Results
docs.text: For all areas of safety testing, we saw major improvements in all categories of content safety relative to previous Gemma models. Overall, Gemma 4 models significantly outperform Gemma 3 and 3n models in improving safety, while keeping unjustified refusals low. All testing was conducted without safety filters to evaluate the model capabilities and behaviors. For both text-to-text and image-to-text, and across all model sizes, the model produced minimal policy violations, and showed significant improvements over previous Gemma models' performance.

docs.title: Usage and Limitations
docs.text: These models have certain limitations that users should be aware of.

docs.title: Intended Usage
docs.text:
Multimodal models (capable of processing vision, language, and/or audio) have a wide range of applications across various industries and domains. The following list of potential uses is not comprehensive. The purpose of this list is to provide contextual information about the possible use-cases that the model creators considered as part of model training and development.

  • Content Creation and Communication
  • Text Generation: These models can be used to generate creative text formats such as poems, scripts, code, marketing copy, and email drafts.
  • Chatbots and Conversational AI: Power conversational interfaces for customer service, virtual assistants, or interactive applications.
  • Text Summarization: Generate concise summaries of a text corpus, research papers, or reports.
  • Image Data Extraction: These models can be used to extract, interpret, and summarize visual data for text communications.
  • Audio Processing and Interaction: The E2B, E4B, and 12B models can analyze and interpret audio inputs, enabling voice-driven interactions and transcriptions.
  • Research and Education
  • Natural Language Processing (NLP) and VLM Research: These models can serve as a foundation for researchers to experiment with VLM and NLP techniques, develop algorithms, and contribute to the advancement of the field.
  • Language Learning Tools: Support interactive language learning experiences, aiding in grammar correction or providing writing practice.
  • Knowledge Exploration: Assist researchers in exploring large bodies of text by generating summaries or answering questions about specific topics.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Training Data
  • The quality and diversity of the training data significantly influence the model's capabilities. Biases or gaps in the training data can lead to limitations in the model's responses.
  • The scope of the training dataset determines the subject areas the model can handle effectively.
  • Context and Task Complexity
  • Models perform well on tasks that can be framed with clear prompts and instructions. Open-ended or highly complex tasks might be challenging.
  • A model's performance can be influenced by the amount of context provided (longer context generally leads to better outputs, up to a certain point).
  • Language Ambiguity and Nuance
  • Natural language is inherently complex. Models might struggle to grasp subtle nuances, sarcasm, or figurative language.
  • Factual Accuracy
  • Models generate responses based on information they learned from their training datasets, but they are not knowledge bases. They may generate incorrect or outdated factual statements.
  • Common Sense
  • Models rely on statistical patterns in language. They might lack the ability to apply common sense reasoning in certain situations.

docs.title: Ethical Considerations and Risks
docs.text:
The development of vision-language models (VLMs) raises several ethical concerns. In creating an open model, we have carefully considered the following:

  • Bias and Fairness
  • VLMs trained on large-scale, real-world text and image data can reflect socio-cultural biases embedded in the training material. Gemma 4 models underwent careful scrutiny, input data pre-processing, and post-training evaluations as reported in this card to help mitigate the risk of these biases.
  • Misinformation and Misuse
  • VLMs can be misused to generate text that is false, misleading, or harmful.
  • Guidelines are provided for responsible use with the model, see the Responsible Generative AI Toolkit.
  • Transparency and Accountability
  • This model card summarizes details on the models' architecture, capabilities, limitations, and evaluation processes.
  • A responsibly developed open model offers the opportunity to share innovation by making VLM technology accessible to developers and researchers across the AI ecosystem.

Risks identified and mitigations:

  • Generation of harmful content: Mechanisms and guidelines for content safety are essential. Developers are encouraged to exercise caution and implement appropriate content safety safeguards based on their specific product policies and application use cases.
  • Misuse for malicious purposes: Technical limitations and developer and end-user education can help mitigate against malicious applications of VLMs. Educational resources and reporting mechanisms for users to flag misuse are provided.
  • Privacy violations: Models were trained on data filtered for removal of certain personal information and other sensitive data. Developers are encouraged to adhere to privacy regulations with privacy-preserving techniques.
  • Perpetuation of biases: It's encouraged to perform continuous monitoring (using evaluation metrics, human review) and the exploration of de-biasing techniques during model training, fine-tuning, and other use cases.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text: At the time of release, this family of models provides high-performance open vision-language model implementations designed from the ground up for responsible AI development compared to similarly sized models.

docs.title: Migrate Lancedb To Chromedb
docs.text:
AnythingLLM comes with a private, built-in vector database powered by LanceDB by default

  1. ChromaDB: The "Developer First" Database

ChromaDB's primary goal is extreme simplicity and rapid prototyping. It handles a massive amount of boilerplate code for you automatically. [1, 2]

  • The Good: It has a "batteries-included" design. Unlike LanceDB, Chroma can accept raw text documents and automatically turn them into embeddings internally using a built-in default framework, taking less than 10 lines of Python code to set up. [1]

  • The Catch: Because its index relies heavily on HNSW algorithms stored directly in your system memory, it eats up a lot of RAM as your database grows. On your 16GB laptop, if you upload massive, thousands-of-pages document libraries, Chroma can start fiercely competing for memory space against your active LLM. [1, 2]

  • LanceDB: The "Performance Lakehouse" Database

LanceDB was written in Rust with a laser focus on low resource overhead, extreme speed, and rich media. [1, 2]

  • The Good: Because it reads data straight from your disk layout using high-performance columnar scanning (benchmarking up to 100x faster than Parquet files), it uses almost no RAM. It will keep your 16GB system incredibly lean. Furthermore, because it natively speaks Apache Arrow, it can easily handle the raw image extractions generated by visual models like your Qwen3-VL-4B. [1, 2, 3]
  • The Catch: It requires you to pass pre-computed vector matrices explicitly (it doesn't auto-embed text by default), and its ecosystem documentation, while growing rapidly, is slightly more developer-centric. [1] Which should you choose for AnythingLLM?

Because AnythingLLM handles all the background configurations for you automatically, your choice depends on what your AI-Librarian is indexing:

  • Choose ChromaDB if you are importing your text-heavy Obsidian Vault markdown notes and want a bulletproof setup that has deep community tracking and instant, out-of-the-box text indexing.
  • Choose LanceDB if you plan to throw heavy PDFs filled with diagrams, screenshots, or textbooks at your system. LanceDB’s disk-centric architecture won't consume your precious laptop memory, leaving the maximum amount of your 16GB RAM wide open for your running Gemma 4 12B model. [1, 2, 3, 4]

==**LanceDB and ChromaDB are not compatible, and AnythingLLM does not support automated data migration between them.

The Re-Embedding Migration Workflow

To migrate your data, you must manually re-index your files. Fortunately, AnythingLLM stores a local copy of your raw files in its internal storage cache, meaning you do not need to re-gather your PDFs or notes from scratch. [1, 2]

The exact manual migration steps include:

  1. Open your workspace's document manager and click the Delete icon next to your uploaded files to clear out the disconnected LanceDB pointers. [1]
  2. Go to Settings > Vector Database and switch the provider from the built-in LanceDB to Chroma. Enter your local Chroma server credentials. [1, 2]
  3. Return to your workspace, select the files from your local storage cache, and click Save and Embed. [1]

Qdrant is a vector database.

Think of it as a specialized database designed for AI search.

Aspect ChromaDB Qdrant Setup complexity Simpler Slightly more complex Footprint Usually smaller Usually larger Personal use Excellent Excellent Enterprise scale Limited Strong Metadata filtering Good Better Performance at large scale Good Excellent Maintenance Lower Higher

docs.title: Migrate To Md
docs.text:
Below is a polished, production‑ready **README.md** you can drop directly into your GitHub repo for your Markdown Migration Tool.

It’s structured for clarity, long‑term maintainability, and GitHub Pages friendliness.

---

# 📘 Markdown Migration Tool

Convert mixed document formats into future‑proof **Markdown (.md)** for Obsidian vaults, GitHub Pages (MkDocs), and long‑term personal knowledge bases.

This tool walks an input directory, detects supported file types, and converts each file into Markdown while preserving folder structure.

---

## 🧩 Features

- Converts multiple formats to Markdown:

- TXT

- RTF

- HTML / HTM / MHT / MHTML

- PDF (text‑based)

- EPUB

- DOCX

- XPS → (manual PDF step required)

- Preserves directory structure

- Creates parallel Markdown output tree

- Uses Pandoc for high‑quality conversion

- Uses Poppler (pdftotext) for PDF extraction

- Optional OCR support for scanned PDFs

- Designed for Obsidian + MkDocs workflows

---

## 📦 Requirements

### **Python 3.8+**

Install from: [https://www.python.org/](https://www.python.org/)

### **Pandoc** (required)

Pandoc performs most conversions.

Install: https://pandoc.org/installing.html [(pandoc.org in Bing)](https://www.bing.com/search?q="https%3A%2F%2Fpandoc.org%2Finstalling.html")

Verify:

pandoc --version

### **Poppler** (required for PDF → text)

Install Windows binaries:

https://github.com/oschwartz10612/poppler-windows/releases/ [(github.com in Bing)](https://www.bing.com/search?q="https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Foschwartz10612%2Fpoppler-windows%2Freleases%2F")

Add poppler/bin to PATH.

Verify:

pdftotext -v

### **Tesseract OCR** (optional, for scanned PDFs)

Install: https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract [(github.com in Bing)](https://www.bing.com/search?q="https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Ftesseract-ocr%2Ftesseract")

Verify:

tesseract --version

---

## 📁 Folder Structure

### **Input directory**

Place your mixed-format documents here:

C:\\Notes\_Input\\

    Recipes\\

    Tech\\

    Home\\

    Health\\

### **Output directory**

The tool creates:

C:\\Notes\_MD\_Output\\

    Recipes\\

    Tech\\

    Home\\

    Health\\

Each file becomes .md with the same relative path.

---

## ▶️ Usage

### **1. Configure paths**

Edit the top of the script:

INPUT\_ROOT = Path(r"C:\\Notes\_Input")

OUTPUT\_ROOT = Path(r"C:\\Notes\_MD\_Output")

### **2. Run the tool**

From PowerShell or CMD:

python migrate\_to\_md.py

### **3. Review output**

Converted Markdown files appear under:

C:\\Notes\_MD\_Output\\

### **4. Move output into your Obsidian vault**

Organize notes into folders, add images, and begin linking inside Obsidian.

### **5. Publish via MkDocs (optional)**

Use MkDocs + GitHub Pages to create a public documentation site.

---

## 🧪 Conversion Examples

### TXT → MD

Plain copy.

### RTF → MD 

pandoc input.rtf -o input.md

### HTML / MHT → MD 

pandoc input.html -o input.md

### PDF → MD 

pdftotext input.pdf temp.txt

pandoc temp.txt -o input.md

### EPUB → MD 

pandoc input.epub -o input.md

### DOCX → MD 

pandoc input.docx -o input.md

### XPS → MD

Manual step:

1. Print XPS → PDF

2. Convert PDF → MD

---

## ⚠️ Limitations

- Scanned PDFs require OCR (Tesseract).

- XPS must be converted to PDF manually.

- Images inside DOCX/HTML/PDF are not extracted in this version.

- Tables convert best from DOCX/HTML; RTF/TXT may lose formatting.

- MHT conversion depends on Pandoc’s HTML extraction quality.

---

## 🚀 Recommended Workflow

1. Convert all documents to Markdown using this tool.

2. Move Markdown files into your Obsidian vault.

3. Organize notes into a simple folder structure.

4. Sync selected folders to GitHub.

Mapping the tasks to specific tools while keeping Ollama as the centralized model warehouse is the exact right way to maximize your 16GB RAM. However, you are missing three critical connection pieces that will bridge your applications (Obsidian, MS Word, and VS Code) directly to your local AI engine. Without these integrations, you will find yourself constantly copying and pasting back and forth, which ruins the workflow.

Here is what you need to add to complete your puzzle:

  1. The Missing Piece for Creative Writing (MS Word Integration)

MS Word cannot natively talk to Ollama. To get Gemma 4 12B to write, brainstorm, or edit directly inside your documents, you need an add-in.

  • The Fix: Install OfficeAI or use the open-source Ollama-Word-Add-in.

  • Alternative Route: If you want a seamless local writing experience without configuring complex Word macros, consider drafting inside Obsidian or LM Studio first, then exporting to Word for final formatting.

  • The Missing Piece for Coding (VS Code Extension)

AnythingLLM is great for chatting about a project, but it doesn't give you inline code completion (like GitHub Copilot) while you type in VS Code.

  • The Fix: Install the Continue.dev or Twinny extension in VS Code.

  • How it completes your stack: You configure the extension to point directly to your background Ollama server. It will use Qwen 2.5 7B to give you lightning-fast, tab-to-complete inline code suggestions and highlighted code refactoring right inside your editor files [sports].

  • The Missing Piece for the AI-Librarian (Obsidian to AnythingLLM Bridge)

Your notes live in Obsidian, but your RAG database lives in AnythingLLM. You need a frictionless way to get your notes indexed by the librarian.

  • The Option A (Manual Sync): Point AnythingLLM's document importer directly to your local Obsidian Vault folder on your hard drive. Whenever you update your notes, you just click "Resync" in AnythingLLM to update Gemma's memory.
  • The Option B (In-Editor AI): If you prefer to stay entirely inside Obsidian, skip AnythingLLM for this specific task and install the Smart Connections or BMO Chatbot plugin inside Obsidian. These plugins allow Gemma 4 12B via Ollama to index your vault and chat with your notes without ever leaving Obsidian.

One Final Hardware Warning for Your i7 CPU

When using VS Code with code-completion extensions, the extension will constantly trigger small AI queries every time you press Enter or pause typing to predict your next line.

Because you are on a CPU-only setup, this can cause a slight typing lag if your CPU process priority isn't managed. Ensure your run-ollama.bat script (with the BelowNormal priority setting we discussed earlier) is running before you open VS Code!

docs.title: Metadata Classifier.Py
docs.text:
``` metadata_classifier.py 11/2/2026 """ metadata_classifier.py 11/2/2026 Author: Charles H Lau

MkDocs Metadata Auto Classifier

Automatically adds YAML front matter metadata to Markdown files within a MkDocs documentation repository.

Features: - Processes Markdown (*.md) files only - Skips index.md files - Skips files that already contain YAML front matter - Generates titles from filenames - Derives category from the first-level folder - Generates tags from the folder hierarchy - Populates created and updated dates from file timestamps - Supports single-file or recursive processing - Provides a dry-run mode for safe previewing

Generated Metadata: title Human-readable title from filename category First folder under docs root tags Folder hierarchy as tag list status Default value: completed created File creation date updated File last modified date

Examples:

Process entire docs tree:
    python metadata_classifier.py --docs docs

Preview changes only:
    python metadata_classifier.py --docs docs --dry-run

Process a single file:
    python metadata_classifier.py \
        --docs docs \
        --file docs/Windows/Hyper-V/virtual_switch_setup.md

Preview a single file:
    python metadata_classifier.py \
        --docs docs \
        --file docs/Windows/Hyper-V/virtual_switch_setup.md \
        --dry-run

Typical Workflow: 1. Import or reorganize notes. 2. Run with --dry-run to review changes. 3. Run without --dry-run to apply metadata. 4. Commit changes to Git.

Use Case: Part of the Personal AI Librarian / Knowledge Management workflow for MkDocs, Obsidian, and AI-assisted note organization. Provides consistent metadata that can later be used for filtering, classification, search, vector databases, and AI-powered knowledge discovery. """

import re import argparse from pathlib import Path from datetime import datetime

def normalize_filename(filename): p = Path(filename)

name = p.stem
name = name.replace(" ", "_")
name = name.replace("-", "_")

while "__" in name:
    name = name.replace("__", "_")

return name + p.suffix

def title_from_filename(filename: str) -> str: name = Path(filename).stem

name = name.replace("_", " ")
name = name.replace("-", " ")

return name.title()

def has_front_matter(content: str) -> bool: lines = content.splitlines()

if len(lines) < 3:
    return False

return lines[0].strip() == "---"

def build_metadata(md_file: Path, docs_root: Path) -> str: rel_path = md_file.relative_to(docs_root)

folders = list(rel_path.parts[:-1])

category = folders[0] if folders else "general"

tags = folders

title = title_from_filename(md_file.name)

stat = md_file.stat()

try:
    created = datetime.fromtimestamp(stat.st_ctime)
except Exception:
    created = datetime.today()

updated = datetime.fromtimestamp(stat.st_mtime)

created_str = created.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
updated_str = updated.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

tag_lines = "\n".join(f"  - {tag}" for tag in tags)

metadata = f"""---

title: {title}

category: {category}

tags:

status: completed

created: {created_str} updated: {updated_str}

"""

return metadata

def process_file(md_file: Path, docs_root: Path, dry_run: bool):

if md_file.suffix.lower() != ".md":
    return

if md_file.name.lower() == "index.md":
    print(f"SKIP (index): {md_file}")
    return

content = md_file.read_text(
    encoding="utf-8",
    errors="ignore"
)

if has_front_matter(content):
    print(f"SKIP (metadata exists): {md_file}")
    return

metadata = build_metadata(md_file, docs_root)

if dry_run:
    print("=" * 60)
    print(md_file)
    print(metadata)
    return

md_file.write_text(
    metadata + content,
    encoding="utf-8"
)

print(f"UPDATED: {md_file}")

def main(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( description="MkDocs Metadata Auto Classifier" )

parser.add_argument(
    "--docs",
    required=True,
    help="Path to docs root"
)

parser.add_argument(
    "--file",
    help="Process a single file"
)

parser.add_argument(
    "--dry-run",
    action="store_true",
    help="Preview changes only"
)

args = parser.parse_args()

docs_root = Path(args.docs).resolve()

if args.file:
    process_file(
        Path(args.file).resolve(),
        docs_root,
        args.dry_run
    )
    return

for md_file in docs_root.rglob("*.md"):
    new_name = normalize_filename(md_file.name)

    if new_name != md_file.name:
        new_path = md_file.with_name(new_name)

        print(f"RENAME: {md_file.name} -> {new_name}")

        if not args.dry_run:
            md_file.rename(new_path)

        md_file = new_path

    process_file(
        md_file,
        docs_root,
        args.dry_run
    )

if name == "main": main()
